item.title: NSPP plasma-water graphene oxide
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported for the lab method (peer-reviewed). Cost, tonne-scale, and “replaces graphite” claims are Preliminary. The 1 Oct 2026 Chemical Engineering item is a recurrence of a paper accepted February 2026.

Related notes: [[guides/glossary|NSPP]] · [[topics/health/form-route|GO]] · [[reference/production]]

Five facts

  1. Banavath et al. grow graphene oxide at a methane–water interface with a non-thermal atmospheric nanosecond pulsed plasma (NSPP). No mined graphite, no Hummers acids.
  2. Journal: Nature Communications, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-69831-0. Received 9 Aug 2025, accepted 9 Feb 2026. Texas A&M plus LTEOIL (College Station).
  3. Reported lab rate: a four-gap reactor up to about 5 g GO per day. That is a bench scale-up, not a plant.
  4. Hydrogen is the co-product. The project started as a hydrogen effort; carbon sheets were the unexpected high-value solid.
  5. Trade coverage on 1 Oct 2026 (Chemical Engineering) restates the July 2026 university release. It is not a new experiment.

What the process is

Conventional GO starts with graphite, oxidizes it (Brodie, Staudenmaier, Hummers and variants), then exfoliates. That route needs concentrated acids and leaves a waste stream.

item.title: Holey graphene as a molecular stencil
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported (peer-reviewed method paper). The mid-September 2026 news cycle is a recurrence, not a new isolation of graphene.

Related notes: [[topics/engineering/2026-09-15-ucla-graphene-stencil]] · [[weekly/2026-W38]] · [[recurrence/log]] · [[timeline/2004]]

If you only remember five facts

  1. The method is a mask: graphene covers gold except at engineered holes; thiol-bearing molecules bind gold in the holes and are blocked where intact graphene sits.
  2. The landmark paper is Thomas et al., ACS Nano 9, 10909 (2015), DOI 10.1021/acsnano.5b03936 — “Holey Graphene as a Weed Barrier for Molecules.”
  3. UCLA Health recirculated the same press framing on 14–15 September 2026. Authors named in that release match the 2015 paper (Paul Weiss, John Thomas, Shan Jiang, Nathan Weiss, Xiangfeng Duan, plus Caltech theory from Gethers and Goddard).
  4. Goal stated by the team: patterned nanoelectronic / biosensor surfaces, including devices small enough in principle to think about recording brain-relevant signals. That is a research aim, not a shipped implant.
  5. Graphene here is used for what it blocks (a chemically quiet lid) as much as for what it conducts.

What “stencil” means in this lab

Chemists have long known how to stick molecules to gold. A thiol (–SH) head group binds Au strongly and can form a self-assembled monolayer (SAM). That is a feature and a problem: gold will accept those molecules almost everywhere the surface is clean. If you want a pattern — molecules only in 20-nanometre-class patches, not a uniform film — you need a mask.

item.title: GO in vaccines / 5G activation claims
item.description:
Evidence: Fringe

Recycled claims that COVID vaccines contain graphene oxide and/or that GO can be “activated” by 5G. Mid-September 2026 posts repeated 2021-era microscopy and petition-hearing material.

Why Fringe

  • Licensed vaccine ingredient lists (FDA, EMA, MHRA and manufacturers) do not include graphene oxide.
  • GO has been used in lab imaging (e.g. cryo-EM) of spike protein — that is not a formulation ingredient.
  • Viral “self-assembly” clips have been traced by fact-checkers to a pre-COVID high-voltage physics demonstration.

See [[weekly/2026-W38]] and [[recurrence/log]].

Evidence: Mixed; tag each row.

Twist / geometry

  • MIT/Harvard Nature (5 Feb 2025 note): first direct superfluid-stiffness measurement in magic-angle graphene; ~10× conventional expectation in that report; temperature dependence read as quantum-geometry.
  • Nature 637, 1084 (22 Jan 2025). Moiré-driven topological electronic crystals in twisted bilayer–trilayer graphene; ν = 1/4 with integer quantum anomalous Hall; Chern number switchable +1/−1.
  • Helical trilayer magnetism, Nat. Phys. (Jan 2025 MIT note).

Fridge stacks. Not powder.

Evidence: Named standards, papers, and RNS. Do not back-fill from a 2026 weekly without the 2024 artifact.

Standards

ISO/TS 80004-13:2024 (Sep 2024) replaces the 2017 vocabulary. Adds GR2M among other revisions. [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Health primary

Andrews et al. 2024 — controlled graphene oxide inhalation in humans (NCT03659864). Form × route row, not a treatment claim. [[topics/health/form-route]]

Industry cash

  • Jun 2024 — Directa Plus ~£6.8–6.9 million at 18p.
  • 30 Apr — NanoXplore C$60 million RBC facility (debt).
  • Nov — Haydale ~£3.1 million + £0.5 million CLN.

[[topics/finance/raises-2015-2025]]

Evidence: Named papers and company notices. Flagship instrument names belong on the Commission page, not a blog paraphrase.

Twist / proximity

  • Zhou et al., Nature 613, 268 (2023). Bernal bilayer graphene + WSe₂: SC at zero field, Tc up ~10× vs the fragile ~30 mK window without WSe₂ in that comparison; density window ~8× wider. Only when the field pushes holes toward WSe₂ (Ising SOC story).
  • Su, Kuiri, et al., Nat. Mater. 22, 1332 (2023). Twisted double bilayer + WSe₂ superconducts in small pockets at 1.24° and 1.37°. TDBG without the dichalcogenide had been the missing cousin.

Still fridge stacks.

Evidence: Named papers and the Haydale RNS. “First order” headlines still need the order text.

Twist

  • Park / Cao / Jarillo-Herrero line, Nat. Mater. 21, 884 (2022) and the MIT “family” note: alternating-twist quadrilayer (and the five-layer cousin) host correlated and superconducting pockets near new magic angles (~1.68° class for ATQG). Family, not a SKU.
  • Kim et al., Nature 606, 494 (2022). STM/STS on magic-angle trilayer: reconstruction toward mirror-symmetric stacking; coherence peaks; doping window that looks like a gap-to-nodal crossover in that paper’s language.

Industry

13 Sep 2022 — Haydale ~£5.51 million. [[topics/finance/raises-2015-2025]]

Evidence: Well-supported for the Nature trilayer paper and for regulator ingredient lists. Fringe for covert-ingredient claims.

Twist

Cao, Park, Watanabe, Taniguchi, Jarillo-Herrero, Nature 595, 526 (2021). Magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene: superconductivity in in-plane fields >10 T, about 2–3× the conventional Pauli limit in that report; re-entrant SC at high field over a narrower density/displacement window. Not predicted from strong spin–orbit. Still three sheets in a fridge. arXiv 2103.12083 (22 Mar); journal 21 Jul.

Evidence: Named papers and the FGR close notice. First-post dates for rumor videos vary by platform.

Twist

  • Stepanov, Das, Lu, et al., Nat. Phys. 16, 926 (2020). Superconductivity in magic-angle bilayer can sit away from the correlated insulators; SC survives larger angle detuning. Competing-phases reading, not “doped Mott like cuprates only.”
  • Cao / Jarillo-Herrero 2020 Nature pair (same week MIT notes): mapping local twist disorder, and a four-layer magic-angle stack more sensitive to E and B than the bilayer. Still a fridge device.

Twisted trilayer Pauli-limit story is 2021. Do not collapse the years.

Evidence: Named 2019 papers. Plant openings stay on [[logs/companies]].

Twist follow-on

  • Yoo, Engelke, et al., Nat. Mater. 18, 448 (2019). Atomic reconstruction in twisted bilayer graphene; crossover near θc ≈ 1° from incommensurate moiré to commensurate domains with soliton walls.
  • Chen, Sharpe, Gallagher, et al., Nature 572, 215 (2019). ABC trilayer graphene / hBN moiré: Mott-like states at 1/4 and 1/2 filling below ~20 K; signatures of tunable superconductivity under a displacement field. Not magic-angle bilayer; a different stack.
  • Mid-2019 STM / spectroscopy cluster on magic-angle bilayer (Kerelsky, Xie, Jiang in Nature; Choi preprint) — maps the flat-band correlations the 2018 transport papers announced.

Still two sheets (or three) in a fridge. Not a tote.

Evidence: Well-supported Nature pair. Vendor claims stay their own class.

Twistronics

Cao, Fatemi, Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues, Nature 556 (2018):

  • 80–84 — correlated insulator at half-filling in magic-angle twisted bilayer (~1.1°).
  • 43–50 — unconventional superconductivity; Tc up to 1.7 K in that report; dome-shaped phase diagram compared to cuprates in the paper’s language.

This is two sheets, a twist, a fridge. It is not PureGRAPH in a tote. Log the idea (twist as a knob) on [[logs/theories]].

Evidence: ISO cover date and Abraham paper. The vocabulary does not certify a bag of powder.

Vocabulary

ISO/TS 80004-13:2017 — first edition September 2017 (ISO); IEC webstore date 14 November 2017. 21 pages. Lists terms for graphene and related 2D materials, production methods, properties, characterization. Withdrawn when 80004-13:2024 replaced it. [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Membranes

Abraham, Vasu, Williams, et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 12, 546 (2017). Physically confined GO laminates; interlayer d tuned ~9.8 Å to 6.4 Å. Ion permeation thermally activated; water less affected. Demo: 97% NaCl rejection in that confined stack. Continuation of Nair 2012, not a municipal plant.

Evidence: Named papers and Flagship dates. Tonnage announcements are not this page.

Policy

April 2016 — Graphene Flagship moves from ramp-up into the first Core project under Horizon 2020. That is a contract phase change, not a product launch. [[timeline/2013]]

Science

  • Ruffieux, Cai, et al., Nature 531, 489 (2016). Bottom-up zigzag-edge graphene nanoribbons on a surface; STS shows edge-localized states. Atomically precise edges in UHV, not a reel of ribbon.
  • Goykhman et al., Nano Lett. 16, 3005 (2016). On-chip silicon–graphene plasmonic Schottky PD; Flagship copy quotes 0.37 A/W at 1.55 µm with avalanche gain. Competes with SiGe in that demo, not a transceiver SKU.
  • Kawai et al., Science 351, 957 (2016). Graphene nanoribbons dragged on gold — superlubricity at 2–200 pN for 5–50 nm ribbons.

Standards weather

ISO/TS 80004-13 lands 2017. 2016 is committee year. [[reference/iso-vocabulary]]

Evidence: Named papers and buildings. Sensor-in-the-brain language is motivation, not a clearance.

Science

  • Thomas et al., ACS Nano 9, 10909 (2015) — holey graphene as a molecular stencil on gold. [[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]]
  • Kim, Yu, Kim, et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 10, 676 (2015). Electrically biased suspended graphene emits bright visible light. Hot electrons ~2,800 K localized because the substrate heat sink is gone; ~1,000-fold thermal-radiation efficiency vs on-SiO₂ mid-IR emitters in that comparison. CVD arrays shown. A lab emitter, not a display SKU.

Institutions

National Graphene Institute (Manchester) opens as a dedicated building.

Evidence: Well-supported papers and listing dates. Product pitches need their own primary.

Listing

April 2014 — Haydale AIM (HAYD). About US$11 million gross in contemporaneous copy; convert the sterling RNS when attaching it. Plasma-functionalization story, not a 4,000 t mill. [[topics/manufacturing/haydale]]

Photodetectors

  • Liu, Chang, Liu, Zhong, Nat. Nanotechnol. 9, 273 (2014). Double-layer graphene heterostructure phototransistor. Room-temperature visible-to-mid-IR; mid-IR responsivity >1 A/W in that report.
  • Koppens, Mueller, Avouris, Ferrari, Vitiello, Polini, Nat. Nanotechnol. 9, 780 (2014). Review of graphene / 2D / hybrid photodetectors — the field’s map after the 2013 waveguide cluster.
  • Cai, et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. (2014) photothermoelectric THz detector: room-temperature THz class, speed claim vs then-existing room-temp THz parts. Still a lab detector.

These sit with 2013 waveguide PDs. None is a catalogue SKU.

Evidence: Commission / Chalmers for the Flagship. AIM notice for AGM. Photonics papers as named.

Flagship dates (do not collapse)

  • 28 January 2013: Graphene named a FET Flagship. Chalmers / Jari Kinaret. Initial ~30-month EC €54 million. GRAPHENE 604391.
  • 10–11 October 2013: kickoff at Chalmers. €1 billion over ten years is a programme class, not a 2013 deposit.

Photonics cluster

September 2013 Nature Photonics cluster (three independent groups in the same issue window):

Evidence: Well-supported device and membrane papers. Market slides stay forecasts.

Devices

  • Britnell et al., Science 335, 947 (2012). Vertical graphene / hBN or MoS₂ / graphene. Room-temperature on/off ~50 (hBN) and ~10,000 (MoS₂) in that prototype.
  • Levendorf et al., Nature 488, 627 (2012). Patterned-regrowth lateral graphene / hBN.
  • Furchi et al., Nano Lett. 12, 2773 (2012). Graphene in a Fabry–Pérot microcavity; absorption pushed above 60% in that geometry; responsivity quoted 21 mA/W. A cavity trick, not a packaged receiver.

Membranes

  • Nair, Wu, Jayaram, Grigorieva, Geim, Science 335, 442 (2012). Sub-micron GO films helium-tight but water almost unimpeded (≥10^10 faster than He in that report). Capillary / humidity story. This is GO laminate, not a 2004 flake with a hole punched in it.
  • Koenig / Bunch line, Nat. Nanotechnol. 7, 728 (2012). UV-oxidative pores in micrometre graphene; H₂, CO₂, Ar, N₂, CH₄, SF₆ leak rates vs effusion model. Lab sieve, not a plant membrane.

Theme

No gap, no CMOS twin. Honest near paths: RF, sensors, photonics, membranes, additives.

Evidence: Well-supported for the IBM device papers. Display ledes attached to a mixer are speculation.

RF

Wu, Lin, Bol, Jenkins, Xia, Farmer, Zhu, Avouris (IBM), Nature 472, 74 (2011) — top-gated CVD graphene RF FETs on diamond-like carbon; gates to 40 nm; f_T to 155 GHz. Different route from the 2010 SiC 100 GHz result.

Circuit

June 2011: IBM graphene frequency mixer on silicon (Science circuit paper). Mixing shown to about 10 GHz. First widely cited circuit, not a phone SoC.

Evidence: Well-supported for prize, Science FET paper, Nature Nanotechnology 30-inch film, and Nature graphene-on-hBN. Prize lectures are not product warranties.

Prize

5 October 2010: Nobel Prize in Physics to Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov “for groundbreaking experiments regarding the two-dimensional material graphene.” Experiments, not the word, not Wallace, not Boehm. Longer note on the same year: this page is the year entry; the older short Nobel page was merged here.

Evidence: Well-supported for the cited papers. GHz and “wafer-scale” in headlines are not a radio product.

Process — copper CVD

Li, Cai, An, Kim, Nah, Yang, Piner, Velamakanni, Jung, Tutuc, Banerjee, Colombo, Ruoff, Science 324, 1312 (2009). Large-area graphene grown by CVD on copper foils, mostly monolayer, transferable. This is the process later fabs and foundries keep trying to industrialize. It does not erase wrinkles, grain boundaries, or transfer polymer residue.

Evidence: Well-supported that growth-on-metal work is underway. Area and uniformity claims need the original figures, not the abstract.

Documented science / process

  • Chemical vapor deposition on nickel and early metal catalysts produces few-layer films that can be transferred. Quality is not yet the later copper-monolayer story ([[timeline/2009]]).
  • Electrochemistry, epitaxial graphene on SiC, and liquid-phase work all run in parallel. There is no single “the graphene process.”

Industry

Patent activity on platelets, inks, and composites is visible. Distinguishing a platelet company from a CVD-film company is already necessary and often skipped in coverage.

Evidence: Well-supported for reviews and the existence of two material families. Performance numbers in press are often best-flake, not average-product.

Documented science

  • Geim and Novoselov, Nature Materials 6, 183 (2007) — the review most later citations treat as the field’s map.
  • Graphene oxide (Hummer’s, Brodie, Staudenmaier routes) and reduced GO are now a parallel literature with different defects, chemistry, and honesty requirements.

Claims in the air

“Stronger than steel, thinner than paper, better than copper” compilations spread. Those comparisons mix ideal monolayer calculations with bulk steel and bulk copper — true as textbook limits, misleading as product copy.

Evidence: Well-supported as a literature-year characterization. Individual “first transistor” headlines vary by definition (field-effect on a flake vs useful circuit).

Documented science

  • Raman spectroscopy (D, G, 2D/G′ bands) becomes the cheap fingerprint for layer number and disorder. Later work will warn that Raman alone does not certify a commercial powder as monolayer graphene.
  • Graphene oxide reduction papers accelerate. Chemists and physicists are still not using the same sample when they say “graphene.”
  • Early FET demonstrations on exfoliated flakes continue the 2004 geometry.

Commercial / program

University groups and a few startups talk transparent conductors as an ITO replacement. ITO replacement will remain a slide more than a market for years. Log specific firms only when a name and filing exist ([[logs/companies]]).

Evidence: Well-supported for the core experiments. Interpretations (“relativistic electrons in a pencil mark”) are pedagogy, not extra data.

Documented science

  • Novoselov, Geim, Morozov, Jiang, Katsnelson, Grigorieva, Dubonos, Firsov, Nature 438, 197 (2005) — two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions in graphene.
  • Zhang, Tan, Stormer, Kim, Nature 438, 201 (2005) — experimental observation of the quantum Hall effect and Berry’s phase in graphene.

Together with [[timeline/2004]], these papers are why Wallace’s 1947 bands ([[timeline/1947]]) stop being a graphite approximation and become a measured monolayer spectrum.

item.title: 2004 — Isolation at Manchester
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

The experiment, without the myth layer

Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov, and collaborators isolate few-layer and monolayer graphene by mechanical cleavage from graphite — the “Scotch tape” method — transfer flakes onto oxidized silicon, and measure an electric-field effect in atomically thin carbon films.

Landmark: Novoselov et al., Science 306, 666 (2004), “Electric field effect in atomically thin carbon films.”

What made 2004 the inflection point was the combination:

item.title: 1962 — Boehm monolayers
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported (with later historiographic argument about what “first graphene” means)

What Boehm’s group reported

Hanns-Peter Boehm and colleagues work from graphite oxide, reduce it, and report extremely thin carbon films, including flakes identified as monolayer. The tools are the TEM / diffraction lineage of mid-century surface and colloid carbon chemistry — not a Hall bar on SiO₂.

Geim and Novoselov have publicly pointed at this line as an experimental precursor. The usual careful wording is:

item.title: 1947 — Wallace band structure
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

The paper-shaped object

P. R. Wallace calculates the electronic band structure of a single layer of graphite in order to understand bulk graphite. Near what are now called the Dirac points (the K and K′ corners of the honeycomb Brillouin zone), the bands are linear. Electrons look massless. That linear dispersion is the theoretical signature people now treat as graphene’s calling card.

Wallace is not writing science fiction about sticky tape. He is doing solid-state theory with a two-dimensional unit as the building block of a three-dimensional crystal.

item.title: Before 1900
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported historical consensus

What “before graphene” actually contains

People used graphite for centuries — marks on surfaces, lubrication, crucibles, later electrodes and moderator blocks. That is three-dimensional stacked carbon. The modern graphene story is not “humanity discovered carbon sheets in 2004.” It is: when did a single honeycomb sheet become an object you could isolate, identify, and measure as a 2D electronic system?

The 19th century answers a different question: when did chemists start taking graphite apart between the layers?

Evidence: Well-supported historical consensus

Crystallography

Early 20th-century X-ray work settles graphite as stacked honeycomb sheets of carbon — a 3D crystal built from 2D units. That picture is what later lets Wallace treat one sheet as a Hamiltonian ([[timeline/1947]]).

Oxide line continues

Brodie-style oxidation does not freeze in 1859. Papers and “graphite oxide paper” products through the 1910s keep the chemical route alive. This is still lamellar oxide, not a gated monolayer device.

Evidence: Well-supported historical consensus

1948 — Ruess and Vogt

Transmission electron microscopy on dried graphene-oxide (graphite-oxide) suspensions shows very thin, creased carbon films. Thickness is in the nanometre class. This is imaging of the oxide route, not a Hall bar.

1950s

Reduction chemistry, ever-thinner flakes, and arguments about how few layers you are actually looking at. The conversation is colloid and surface carbon, sitting next to growing graphite-moderator and electrode industries.

item.title: 1963-2003 — Name, epitaxy, near misses
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported historical papers. Not “graphene was invented in 2004” and not “2004 was nothing.”

Naming

Mid-1980s, often cited as 1986: Boehm, Setton, Stumpp and colleagues fix graphene as the systematic name for a single graphite sheet (graphite + -ene). The word is older in talk; this is the nomenclature paper trail. [[timeline/1962]] · [[guides/glossary]]

Epitaxy that is real and stuck

  • Metal surfaces: monolayer carbon on Ni, Ru, Pt and cousins through the 1960s–1990s surface-science literature (LEED, AES, later STM). Land, Michely, Behm-type STM on Ru is the picture people remember from the early 1990s.
  • SiC: Van Bommel, Crombeen, Van Tooren, Surf. Sci. (1975) — heating SiC sublimes Si and leaves carbon-rich layers. That is epitaxial graphene on a wafer, usually not a gated flake on SiO₂.

These layers matter. They are a different object from the 2004 transferred/exfoliated FET. [[timeline/2004]]

item.title: 2005–2009 — Dirac physics and a research gold rush
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported

Science

  • 2005: Transport and spectroscopy lock in graphene carriers as massless Dirac fermions — Wallace’s picture on a real flake ([[timeline/1947]], [[timeline/2004]]).
  • Quantum Hall work, Raman fingerprints (D/G/2D), and early CVD on metals become community habits.
  • Citation explosion. Labs stand up graphene groups as a default, not a novelty.

Industry seeds

Early companies and patents around nanoplatelets, transparent conductors, composites. Specialist press (e.g. Graphene-Info from 2009) starts the weekly-vendor drumbeat that still shapes 2026 coverage. Log first appearances on [[logs/companies]] when a named firm or product line is documented.

item.title: 2011–2012 — Post-Nobel acceleration
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at program level

CVD on copper plus transfer methods become the default film story. Flexible electronics, RF transistors, and photonics demos multiply. EU policy talk hardens toward a Flagship ([[timeline/2013]]).

The era’s idea — graphene replaces silicon — collides with band gap, contact resistance, and uniformity. File that ideal on [[logs/theories]]. Do not treat a 2011 keynote as a 2026 product.

Next

[[timeline/2013]]

item.title: 2014–2019 — Roadmaps, pilots, early products
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at overview level

Powders/platelets and CVD films increase. Niches that actually ship something: composites, coatings, additives, thermal interface materials, conductive inks, sports-equipment demos. “Graphene” on a label is not a monolayer guarantee — ISO/IEC terminology fights start here.

Research attention partly shifts to van der Waals heterostructures and other 2D crystals. The stencil paper ([[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]], 2015) sits in this window: graphene as a process tool, not a silicon killer.

item.title: Bio-mechanical
item.description:
Parent: [[topics/medical]]. Human device and exposure rows already filed: [[topics/health/biomedical-catalogue]]. Patterning paper: [[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]].

Already on this archive

  • INBRAIN cortical interface, NCT06368310 — first-in-human intraoperative use; small set; Preliminary device data. [[topics/health/effects]]
  • Graphene / GO / GFET electrode and biosensor literature — high paper count, few cleared instruments.
  • Oriented GO/PCL fibres and conductive scaffolds — rat sciatic-gap and in-vitro axon-length reports. Animal. Preliminary translation.
  • Holey graphene as a molecular stencil on gold (2015) — fabrication toward sensors, not an implant.
  • Directa G+ textile membranes and printed thermal circuits — garments, not implants. [[topics/industry/directa-gplus]]
  • ZenGUARD on mask and HVAC media — coat on a filter, not a neural thread. [[topics/industry/zenguard]]

Goals people write down

  • A cortical or peripheral electrode that records or stimulates without a stainless-steel penalty in flexibility or site area.
  • A scaffold that is conductive enough for cells and resorbable enough for a surgeon.
  • A wearable (tattoo, textile, microneedle) that lasts a shift, not a press cycle.
  • Closed-loop interfaces. Still a review-article sentence in 2025–26.

Theories in circulation

  • “Graphene replaces silicon in diagnostics this decade.” Same foundry problem as the electronics pitch. [[logs/theories]]
  • A patterning paper “will treat” a named disease this cycle. Motivation language. [[logs/unsourced]]
  • Long-term implant / IV GO is solved. 2025–26 reviews still list cytotoxicity, dose, metals, and fate as open.

Projections (forecast language)

Patient-specific printed grafts, smart microneedles, injectable graphene, AI-designed scaffolds — review-article futures. They sit next to the NCT table, not in place of it.

  • Form × route matrix. [[topics/health/form-route]]
  • Occupational and small-human effects. [[topics/health/effects]]
  • Andrews 2024 / NCT03659864 GO inhalation — acute physiology, not ecology.
  • Rodent high-dose lung inflammation / fibrosis trend in some designs — size, oxidation, metals, respirable fraction. Same effects page.
  • In-vitro antibacterial / antiviral GO pile — large, condition-dependent. [[topics/health/biomedical-catalogue]]
  • GO as a carrier in cells and rodents (small-molecule, photothermal ideas) — delivery papers, not licensed drugs.

Goals people write down

  • A sheet that a cell treats as inert at a useful dose.
  • A sheet that a microbe does not ignore (antibacterial coatings, filter media — [[topics/industry/zenguard]] is a coat, not a drug).
  • Fate and clearance maps for GO vs rGO vs GNP after lung, gut, or skin contact.
  • Plant and soil studies that survive a second lab.

Theories in circulation

  • “Pencil lead, therefore biology is done.” Ignores GO vs monolayer vs powder. [[reference/misconceptions]]
  • “One IC50 in a dish predicts a workplace or a vaccine.” Wrong evidence class. [[topics/fringe]]
  • Oxidative-stress / sharp-edge cutting as the mechanism. Real papers exist; they do not collapse to one slogan.
  • Bioaccumulation as a cover-up story. Documented on [[logs/conspiracies]], not here as fact.

Projections (forecast language)

Reviews keep projecting biodegradable graphene, DNA–graphene scaffolds, and “green” GO from biomass. Treat as slides until there is an NCT number or a regulator text. Market-size “graphene healthcare” figures stay [[logs/unsourced]] unless the house and the definition are quoted.

item.title: Conspiracy and fringe-narrative log
item.description:
Not a truth list. Documenting a start date is not endorsing the claim.

Two different problems live on this tab:

  1. Fringe — a conspiracy-style narrative (plot, hidden ingredient, activation, cover-up).
  2. Unsourced — a factual-sounding claim with no solid primary source. It may be ordinary hype, a rumor, or a press sentence that cannot be opened. It is not automatically a conspiracy.

Theories and companies stay elsewhere: [[logs/theories]] · [[logs/companies]].

Fringe narratives

When the narrative takes form Claim Label Notes Pages

Experimental GO as an animal-model adjuvant is a real research topic. Do not file it as a conspiracy, and do not file it as proof about licensed human vaccines.

item.title: Forms of the graphene family
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported as materials taxonomy. A bag labeled “graphene” is not thereby a 2004 Manchester flake.

If one page on this site should survive a server migration, it is this one. Most arguments about graphene are arguments about which solid.

Pristine sheets

  • Monolayer graphene — one honeycomb plane of sp² carbon. The object of [[timeline/2004]] and [[timeline/1947]].
  • Bilayer / few-layer (FLG) — two to roughly ten planes. Electronic structure changes with layer number and stacking. Magic-angle twisted bilayer is a stacking-and-angle story ([[timeline/2018]]), not a powder grade.
  • Graphite — many planes, 3D crystal. Parent material ([[timeline/pre-chemistry]]).

Chemically derived

  • Graphite oxide — oxidized, lamellar graphite (Brodie lineage, [[timeline/before-1900]]).
  • Graphene oxide (GO) — exfoliated oxidized sheets; hydrophilic; insulating compared with graphene; processable in water.
  • Reduced graphene oxide (rGO) — GO with oxygen stripped back. More conductive than GO, more defective than cleaved or good CVD graphene.

Industrial grades (names vary by vendor)

  • Nanoplatelets / GNP — stacks that may be tens of layers. Often what “tonnes of graphene” means.
  • CVD film — grown on metal (Cu landmark: [[timeline/2009]]), transferred. Grain boundaries and wrinkles are part of the object.
  • Epitaxial graphene on SiC — carbon left after Si leaves the surface. IBM 100 GHz FETs used this family ([[timeline/2010]]).
  • Graphene quantum dots (GQDs) — very small pieces with confined electronics and photoluminescence claims; quality varies wildly.
  • Foams, aerogels, fibres, yarns — assembled architectures (e.g. wet-spun GO fibres in [[weekly/2026-W38]]).
  • Holey / perforated graphene — engineered holes; mask or membrane, not a synonym for GO ([[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]]).

Naming collisions

  • Graphene monoxide / eCOphite — company chemistry ([[topics/finance/2026-09-15-conovate-doe-award]]), not GO.
  • “Graphene battery” in a headline may mean a conductive additive, a coating, an anode experiment, or wishful copy.

See [[reference/misconceptions]] and [[guides/glossary]].

item.title: Health by form and route
item.description:
Not medical advice. Pair with [[topics/health/effects]] and [[reference/safety]].

Dry GNP / nanoplatelet powder — workplace air

  • Primary: NIOSH field work in US graphene plants. Respirable elemental carbon from below 0.01 µg/m³ to about 1,825 µg/m³. Conservative evaluation band often cited near <10 µg/m³ (not an OSHA PEL). Many dry-powder samples sat above that band.
  • Label: Well-supported as hygiene measurements. Not a human disease study.
  • [[topics/policy/2026-09-16-niosh-graphene-exposure]]

Thin purified GO aerosol — short controlled human inhalation

  • Primary: Andrews JPM et al. Nat. Nanotechnol. 19, 705–714 (2024). doi:10.1038/s41565-023-01572-3. NCT03659864.
  • What they did: 14 young healthy volunteers; double-blind randomized visits; small and ultrasmall GO vs filtered air; 200 µg/m³ for 2 h.
  • What they reported: exposure tolerated; heart rate, blood pressure, lung function, inflammatory markers not changed by size in that window; mild signal in an ex vivo thrombus model; authors: no overt acute cardiorespiratory harm in this design.
  • Label: Preliminary human, one acute protocol. Not chronic shop air. Not GNP powder.

GrapheneBlack-class powder — guideline tox package (not a volunteer trial)

  • Primary trail: company-commissioned package on GrapheneBlack 3X summarized in open literature (e.g. 2020 crystals paper discussing Charles River work): dermal, acute inhalation, genotox endpoints with no adverse finding at the doses they ran; inhalation NOAEL language at the maximum achieved aerosol they could generate.
  • Label: Preliminary product-specific animal/in vitro package. Not NIOSH field air. Not Andrews GO.

GO / rGO — rodent lung, high dose

  • Primary pile: Graphene Flagship toxicology stream, collected in Fadeel et al. ACS Nano 12, 10582–10620 (2018) and the 2025 Flagship lessons paper Fadeel et al. Small 21, 2404570 (2025), PMC11840464.
  • Flagship takeaway they print: GBMs are not one material; they did not find “excessive or alarming” toxicity in the tested set; realistic life-cycle exposure still thin.
  • Older high-dose rodent lung papers still show inflammation and, in some protocols, fibrotic trend — size, metals, oxidation decide which paper you are holding.
  • Label: Preliminary / mixed animal. Cite the specific paper, not “graphene.”

Skin

  • Flagship / banding reviews: limited uptake for the thin GO sheets they tested; macrophages can internalize thin GO without the “blade cutting the cell” slogan holding up in later Flagship work (Fadeel 2025 discussion of earlier membrane-piercing citations).
  • GrapheneBlack 3X dermal package: no adverse finding at tested doses (company-commissioned trail above).
  • Label: Preliminary. Gloves in a powder shop are still hygiene, not a fashion choice.

Swallowed or IV “GO medicine”

  • No Phase I/II therapeutic of raw GO as a licensed drug in 2026-era reviews we log.
  • Label: Well-supported as a negative for the slogan. Delivery-vehicle papers are a different object — name the construct.

rGO / graphene film on an electrode — intraoperative cortex

  • Registry: NCT06368310. INBRAIN Graphene Cortical Interface during tumor resection. Manchester / Northern Care Alliance. Actual start 6 Aug 2024.
  • Interim company/meeting trail (first 4 patients): no device-related adverse events in that set; high-gamma / phoneme-linked activity claimed during awake mapping. Meeting abstract: Coope et al., SURG-92 style interim.
  • Label: Preliminary device. Not powder toxicology. [[topics/health/biomedical-catalogue]]

Composite in a tire, paint, or shirt

  • Not evidence of monolayer in blood.
  • Label: Category error if used that way. [[logs/unsourced]]

Licensed vaccine ingredient lists

  • Do not include GO.
  • Label: Well-supported as a negative. Plot versions: [[logs/conspiracies]] · [[topics/fringe/2026-09-16-go-vaccine-5g-claims]]

Still empty on purpose

Chronic low-dose human inhalation of shop powder. Occupational disease clusters. Gut and IV fate by exact commercial grade. Those are gaps.

item.title: Health effects
item.description:
Graphene-family materials are not one toxicology object. GO ≠ cleaved monolayer ≠ dry nanoplatelet powder. [[reference/forms]] · [[reference/safety]] · [[notice|Notice]]

Humans

  • Worker disease cluster at graphene plants: reviews used by NIOSH still report no known case series in GFN workers. Absence of reports ≠ lifelong proof.
  • Controlled GO inhalation (Andrews et al. 2024; NCT03659864): ~14 volunteers, ~2 h at ~200 µg/m³ thin purified GO; no acute change in the markers they tracked. Preliminary; one dose; hours of follow-up.
  • Graphene cortical electrodes (NCT06368310, INBRAIN): first-in-human intraoperative set; early writeups of usable signal, no device-linked serious events in that set. Preliminary device data.
  • GO as a licensed drug or vaccine ingredient: 2026-era reviews and licensed lists do not name GO. Well-supported as a negative for the slogan.

Animals and cells

High-dose rodent lung protocols can inflame and, in some designs, trend fibrotic. Outcome tracks size, thickness, oxidation, metals, respirable fraction. A cell-culture IC50 is not an occupational limit.

item.title: How graphene-family materials are made
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported as a process map. Capacity announcements are not grades.

Mechanical cleavage

Scotch-tape / micromechanical exfoliation from graphite. Best flakes for physics. Terrible area. [[timeline/2004]]

Epitaxy on SiC

Heat SiC; Si leaves; carbon rearranges. Wafer-ish, substrate-bound, expensive. IBM 100 GHz FETs ([[timeline/2010]]).

CVD on metal

Grow on Cu (landmark [[timeline/2009]]) or Ni; transfer off. Path to large optical films ([[timeline/2010]] Bae). Defects: grains, wrinkles, transfer residue, cracks.

Oxide route

Oxidize graphite (Brodie / Staudenmaier / Hummers), exfoliate to GO, optionally reduce to rGO. Scalable, dirty, hydrophilic. [[timeline/before-1900]] · [[timeline/1962]]

item.title: ISO and IEC graphene wording
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported that these documents exist and carry these years. Clause text lives in the paid file.

Parent: [[reference/index]] · [[guides/glossary]] · [[timeline/2017]]

Vocabulary

  • ISO/TS 80004-13:2017 — Nanotechnologies — Vocabulary — Part 13: Graphene and related two-dimensional materials. First edition.
  • ISO/TS 80004-13:2024 — Second edition (Sep 2024). Cancels 2017. Adds graphene-related 2D material (GR2M) among other revisions. Joint ISO/IEC circulation in the draft trail.
  • Related core vocab still cited by those parts: ISO/TS 80004-1 (core terms), 80004-2 (nano-objects), 80004-6 (nano-object characterization).

Structural characterization of powders and dispersions

  • ISO/TS 21356-1:2021 (first edition, March 2021). Sequence of methods after isolating flakes: layer number / thickness, lateral size, disorder, layer alignment, specific surface area. Covers graphene, bilayer, nanoplatelets from powder or liquid. Raman, SEM, AFM, TEM, BET in the usual toolkit. CEN adopted as CEN ISO/TS 21356-1:2022.

How this site maps the words

Site word We mean Do not hear
Graphene Honeycomb sheet; say monolayer if we mean one layer Any black powder
FLG A few layers, when the paper counts them GO paper
GNP / nanoplatelet Thicker stack sold as graphene 2004 Manchester flake
GO Oxidized sheets from graphite oxide Vaccine antigen
rGO GO with oxygen pulled back Defect-free CVD
CVD film Grown then often transferred 4,000 t powder
GR2M ISO 2024 umbrella for graphene-related 2D materials A new allotrope

What a standard is not

Not a bag certificate. Not a health clearance. Not proof a vendor is “ISO graphene certified” because the letters appear on a slide.

item.title: Pre-chemistry — graphite before laboratories
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported at the level of mining and craft history; specific ancient identifications of “graphite vs molybdenite vs galena” are often later reconstructions.

What this page is

Before there is a chemist named Brodie, there is a slippery black solid people write with and grease with. They do not have the word graphene. They often do not even have a clean distinction between graphite and look-alike minerals.

This is the floor of the timeline. Monday posts can start here when the hook is “graphene is new; carbon sheets are not.”

item.title: Properties — ideal sheet vs real sample
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported that the ideal monolayer has extraordinary calculated and measured properties. Transferring those numbers onto a painted wall or a 1 Ah cell is a separate claim.

Electronic

  • Linear bands near the Dirac points ([[timeline/1947]], [[timeline/2005]]).
  • High mobility on good samples, especially encapsulated on hBN ([[timeline/2010]], [[timeline/2012]]).
  • No native band gap in monolayer graphene. That is why digital-logic replacement of silicon stalled as an engineering ideal ([[timeline/2011]], [[logs/theories]]).
  • Bilayers, nanoribbons, and certain stacks can open gaps — different objects.

Mechanical

  • Intrinsic strength and stiffness of a pristine monolayer are among the highest measured for a 2D crystal (Lee / Hone Science 2008 nanoindentation is the usual citation). A polymer with 0.1 wt% platelets does not inherit that tensile strength.

Thermal / optical

  • High in-plane thermal conductivity on clean samples; grain boundaries, wrinkles, and matrix interfaces dominate real heat-spreader products.
  • Visible transparency of a monolayer is ~97.7% (Nair et al., Science 2008 is the usual optical landmark). That number made transparent-electrode pitches easy to write ([[timeline/2010]] Bae film).

Chemical

  • Basal plane is relatively inert; edges and defects are where chemistry happens. That is why a stencil on gold is about holes and edges ([[posts/holey-graphene-molecular-stencil]]) and why GO is a different substance.

Rule for readers

Ask: which form ([[reference/forms]]), how measured, in what matrix, at what loading. If a press release quotes the ideal monolayer next to a bulk product, that is rhetoric.

item.title: Related 2D materials
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported that these crystals are studied in the same labs and programmes (Flagship mandate included “related layered materials”: [[timeline/2013]]).

  • hBN — insulating honeycomb; the preferred encapsulant / substrate for clean graphene transport ([[timeline/2010]] Dean).
  • TMDCs (MoS₂, WS₂, …) — many have a band gap; different electronics than graphene.
  • Phosphorene, silicene, MXenes, etc. — separate literatures. Mention when a source actually uses them; do not absorb them into “graphene news.”

Twisted stacks and heterostructures are how these combine ([[timeline/2012]], [[timeline/2018]]).

item.title: Safety, exposure, toxicology
item.description:
Evidence: Mixed. Field hygiene data can be well-supported. Many cell-culture papers are preliminary. Nothing here is medical advice.

Full effects table (humans, animals, workplace numbers): [[topics/health/effects]].

What is actually measured at work

NIOSH sampled workers at US graphene producers/users. Against a conservative 10 µg/m³ occupational band (not an OSHA PEL), many samples exceeded it when dry powder was handled. Prefer masterbatch or liquid in that literature. [[topics/policy/2026-09-16-niosh-graphene-exposure]] · [[weekly/2026-W38]]

No disease cluster is attached to those notes on this site. Absence of a reported cluster is not proof of lifelong safety.

item.title: Spray and weather
item.description:
Parent: [[topics/fringe]]. Label on this column is Fringe unless a primary says otherwise.

What circulates

  • Aircraft contrails recast as “chemtrails” that contain graphene or GO.
  • Weather-control or solar-geoengineering programmes said to spray graphene as the payload.
  • The same payload then tied to 5G, vaccines, or livestock deaths in one thread.

What the public record actually holds

  • Graphene-family powders are made in plants and labs. That is [[topics/manufacturing/directory]].
  • Occupational air samples exist at some of those plants. That is [[topics/health/effects]] (NIOSH field notes).
  • There is no regulator text on this shelf that treats graphene as an authorized aerial-spray climate tool.
  • A toxicity paper in rodents is not a flight log. [[reference/safety]]

Why it stays on Fringe

The jump is always the same: a real material + a real high-dose paper + a photograph of a sky → a programme. The middle step is missing. Missing citation = [[logs/unsourced]]. A cover-up story = this column.

item.title: Standards and quality
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported that ISO/IEC vocabulary and related technical specs exist. They do not certify a random SKU.

Why this page exists

After ~2014, “graphene” on an invoice could mean almost any of [[reference/forms]]. Purchasing fights are about layer number, lateral size, oxygen content, metal residue, and surface area — not Dirac cones.

Documented landmarks

  • ISO/TS 80004-13:2017 — vocabulary for graphene and related two-dimensional carbons ([[timeline/2017]]). Its value is admitting multiple materials.
  • National measurement labs (NPL and peers) publish characterization good-practice notes (Raman, XPS, AFM, TGA). Use the lab document, not a tweet summarizing it.
  • Flagship and national projects spent years on protocols; protocols ≠ enforcement.

Practical reader checklist

  1. Which form?
  2. Layer distribution, not a single magic number.
  3. Oxygen / defect metric (XPS, Raman D/G).
  4. Metals and residual solvent.
  5. Dry powder vs masterbatch ([[topics/policy/2026-09-16-niosh-graphene-exposure]]).

If a vendor will not answer those, the archive can still list the press release — under Preliminary or Unverified.

  • Jul 2025: company said it could not sell certain UK technology assets; expected Versarien Graphene Ltd into administration; Cambridge Graphene Ltd and 2-DTech Ltd toward voluntary liquidation; Korea ops ceased (Graphene-Info recap of the RNS).
  • Companies House: Versarien Graphene Limited (07475659) — administrator appointed Aug 2025; registered office moved to Leonard Curtis, Manchester.
  • 6 Jan 2026: Versarien plc joint administrators Andrew Knowles and Andrew Poxon (Leonard Curtis). Shares had been suspended. Remaining assets in that notice: patents/trademarks plus shareholdings in Total Carbide Ltd and Gnanomat SL, described as still trading solvent.

File here as history until a buyer of the graphene kit files a new operating address.
